messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Malik was eight years old when he first learned how silence could mean something terrible was about to happen. He was standing in the hallway of his family’s apartment, one hand pressed flat against the wall, the other clamped over his own mouth so his mother wouldn’t hear him cry. The living room was quiet—a heavy, waiting silence that pressed against his ears. Then his father’s voice, low and grinding, and then the sound of something hitting the wall. Malik remembers that moment as a picture in his mind: the crack in the plaster, the overturned lamp, his mother’s face turned away. He remembers his own body, frozen behind the door, arms locked at his sides, every muscle rigid. Even now, when a memory of that night comes back, his body goes into that exact position—shoulders hunched, breath held, as if he is still hiding. And the grief that follows is overwhelming, a bottomless sadness for his mother that feels as fresh as it did a decade ago.

As Malik grew older, the feeling of helplessness hardened into a belief: he could not stop bad things from happening to people he loved. He had stood there and done nothing. He began to scan every room for danger before he could feel safe—noticing where a knife sat on a counter, how a stranger’s hand rested near his pocket, the way a person’s eyes moved when they spoke. By the time he became a police officer at eighteen, that vigilance felt like an asset. He told himself he would be the one who saw the threat first, who would never be caught off guard again.

But the job has made everything worse. Malik now spends his shifts in unfamiliar houses, hallways, basements—places whose layouts he cannot predict, where danger could be in any corner. Every call feels like stepping into that hallway again. When he enters a home and the residents go silent, his heart slams against his ribs because he knows that silence: it means something is about to break. He sees potential weapons everywhere—a beer bottle on a coffee table, a screwdriver on the kitchen counter—and his eyes lock onto them before he can even hear what the dispatcher is saying. He has come to believe that he cannot rely on himself to stay calm. More than once, his partner has had to touch his shoulder to get his attention during a quiet scene, and Malik has flinched hard, his hand flying to his holster. That unexpected touch, when he is not prepared for it, sends a jolt through his whole body—the same jolt he felt when his father’s fist connected with the wall near his mother’s head.

Malik has started to avoid places he does not already know. Off-duty, he stays mostly at home. He will not go to a new restaurant or a friend’s apartment unless he can visit it first in daylight, alone, to map the exits. He tells himself he needs to assess the danger, but the logic feels thin. What frightens him most is the feeling that his own mind is no longer trustworthy—that his reactions since that night mean he is going crazy. He has never told anyone about the snapshots that intrude at random moments: his mother’s flinch, the frame of the door, the crack in the plaster. When they come, his body acts as if it is still there, and he has to excuse himself from the room to stand in the hallway alone until the feeling passes.

What finally brought Malik to seek help was a domestic violence call three weeks ago. He walked into a living room, saw a woman with her arm raised protectively across her face, and he stopped cold. His body locked into that childhood position—arms at his sides, breath stopped—and he could not move or speak. His partner handled the situation, but afterward Malik sat in the squad car shaking, flooded with grief and the old helplessness. He is afraid that he will freeze again on a call and someone will get hurt. He is afraid that his captain will notice, that he will be seen as unfit. But underneath that, he is hoping that someone can explain why a memory that is ten years old still has hold of his body, and whether there is a way to let go.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Helplessness: The symptom 'Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me' is not reflected. The vignette describes helplessness about bad things happening to loved ones, not to the patient himself.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

When they come, his body acts as if it is still there, and he has to excuse himself from the room to stand in the hallway alone until the feeling passes. The helplessness he felt as a boy—the certainty that he could not protect himself—has never left. It follows him into every unfamiliar room, every quiet moment, every split second when his hand moves toward his holster before his mind can catch up.
